newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Crop slips but exports look fine.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Crop slips but exports look fine.

text.p: Expectations of Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop continue to slide as dry weather continues, senior officials in the Australian grains industry say.

In meetings with industry representatives in three days of Australian Wheat Board (AWB) Grain Leaders sessions in the second half of last week, senior figures in Australia's grains industry said the view was settling that Australia would produce a wheat crop of less than 15.0 million tonnes.
This is down from a revised forecast of 15 to 16 million tonnes by the AWB in July.
Earlier in the year, the AWB had made a preliminary forecast of 18 million tonnes. Australia's wheat production in 1996/97 was a record 23.5 million tonnes.
Latest views put the wheat crop at lower than the range of official forecasts for the drought-hit wheat crop.

Private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd has the likely crop at 17.85 million tonnes, while the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics is forecasting the crop at 16.3 million tonnes.

Western Australia, which unlike the rest of Australia has had good opening rain for the crop, is now expected to set a clear lead over the rest of Australia, producing up to seven million tonnes against about 4.0 million from New South Wales.
Last season, NSW was clear production leader, on about 8.6 million tonnes against about 7.7 million tonnes in WA.

But sessions in the Grains Leaders meetings indicated that half a million tonnes of wheat one way or another was less significant in the longer-term than factors such as the AWB's retention of its single desk monopoly on wheat exports and the emergence of new competitors such as Argentina.
AWB general manager international Nigel Officer said one clear example of the value of the single desk was shown in recent problems with the sale of two million tonnes of wheat contracted by India.
Australia's negotiations with India to overcome objections to seed weed in early shipments was made possible by the AWB's longer-term view through its single desk powers, he said.
A longer-term approach through its single desk also paved the way for the AWB to access the Taiwan wheat market from which Australia had been absent for about 10 years, he said.
Taiwan takes about 60,000 to 100,000 tonnes of Australian wheat a year.
Officer backed up this view by pointing out that the export market, for Australia, "is everything". Australia was likely headed for exports of about 11.5 million tonnes in the current year, he said.
Exports represent about 80 percent of Australia's annual wheat output, against only about 43 percent of U.S. production.
This gave Australia a 16.8 percent share of the world market in 1996/97 against 23.9 percent by the U.S. and a doubled share by Argentina, at 9.75 percent.
Argentina would remain a rising force on world markets, he also said.

Argentina's rise as a wheat exporter is seen as all the more significant for Australia because Argentina's adoption of product segregation and plans to move into branded wheat -- following moves by the AWB.
Australia remained in a strong position to export in the current year, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
